# Page 4^page=4
The transformation rule

# Page 5^page=5
Recall: Covariant and contravariant components Covariant and contravariant components Using dual bases, we have found that a vector A can be expanded with respect to the vectors of one basis e1, e2, e3 via A = A1e1 + A2e2 + A3e3 = A iei. with respect to the vectors of the dual basis e1, e2, e3 via A = A1e 1 + A2e 2 + A3e 3 = Aie i. Recall that Ai = A · ei are called the contravariant components of A, and Ai = A · ei are called the covariant components of A. 2 27

# Page 6^page=6
Different coordinate systems Coordinate systems Let e1, e2, e3 and e′ 1, e′ 2, e′ 3 be bases of two coordinate systems. In the system de˝ned by e1, e2, e3, let A have covariant components Ai and contravariant components Ai, that is A = Aiei = Aie i. In the system de˝ned by e′ 1, e′ 2, e′ 3, let A have covariant components A′ i and contravariant components A′i, that is A = A′iei = A′ ie i. How do we transform the components from one coordinate system to another? 3 27

# Page 7^page=7
Transforming between coordinate systems - Coefficients of expansions Coe˚cients of expansions First, let L1 i′, L2 i′, L3 i′ be the coe˚cients of the expansion of e′ i with respect to the vectors e1, e2, e3, that is e ′ 1 = L 1 1′e1 + L 2 1′e2 + L 3 1′e3 e ′ 2 = L 1 2′e1 + L 2 2′e2 + L 3 2′e3 e ′ 3 = L 1 3′e1 + L 2 3′e2 + L 3 3′e3 or more concisely e ′ i = L j i′ej. 4 27

# Page 8^page=8
Transforming between coordinate systems - Coefficients of expansions - Part 2 Coe˚cients of expansions Let us ˝nd an expression for Lj i′. Here, we are working in vector notation . Since e ′ i = 3∑ k=1 L k i′ek and ek · e j = δik, (dual basis) we see that e ′ i · e j = ( 3∑ k=1 Lk i′ek ) · e j = 3∑ k=1 Lk i′ (ek · e j) = 3∑ k=1 L k i′δkj = L j i′. Similarly, we can ˝nd the inverse transformation L j′ i = ei · e ′j. 5 27

# Page 9^page=9
Transformation rule for the covariant components Transformation rule for the covariant components If we start with an expansion A = Ajej, and take the dot product with e′ i, we get A · e ′ i = (Aje j) · e ′ i = Aj(e ′i · e j) = L j i′Aj (L j i′ = e ′ i · e j) In other words, the covariant component A′ i is given by A′ i = A · e ′ i = L j i′Aj. This is the transformation rule for the covariant components. 6 27

# Page 10^page=10
Transformation rule for the contravari- ant components Transformation rule for the contravariant components Similarly, if we start with an expansion A = Ajej, and take the dot product with e′i, we get A · e ′i = (Aje ′ j) · e i = Aj(e i · e ′ j) = L i j′Aj (L i j′ = e i · e ′j) In other words, the contravariant component A′i is given by A ′i = A · e ′i = L i j′Aj. This is the transformation rule for the contravariant components. 7 27

# Page 11^page=11
The transformation rule The transformation rule The transformation rule for the covariant components is A′ i = Lj i′Aj. The transformation rule for the contravariant components is A ′i = L i′ j Aj. Task Verify the inverse formulas Ai = L j′ i A′ j, Ai = L i j′A′j. 8 27

# Page 12^page=12
Example Example Let K be a coordinate system with orthonormal basis i1, i2, i3. Let K′ be a new coordinate system with basis vectors e ′ 1 = i1, e ′ 2 = 2i2, e ′ 3 = i1 + i3. Let us ˝nd the expansion coe˚cients L1 i′, L2 i′, L3 i′ for each i = 1, 2, 3. We have Ln m′ = e′ m · in, thus L 1 1′ = e ′ 1 · i1 = i1 · i1 = 1, L 1 2′ = e ′ 2 · i1 = 2i2 · i1 = 0. 9 27

# Page 13^page=13
Example - Part 2 Example Let K be a coordinate system with orthonormal basis i1, i2, i3. Let K′ be a new coordinate system with basis vectors e ′ 1 = i1, e ′ 2 = 2i2, e ′ 3 = i1 + i3. Let us ˝nd the expansion coe˚cients L1 i′, L2 i′, L3 i′ for each i = 1, 2, 3. We have Ln m′ = e′ m · in, thus L 1 1′ = 1, L 2 1′ = 0, L 3 1′ = 0, L 1 2′ = 0, L 2 2′ = 2, L 3 2′ = 0, L 1 3′ = 1, L 2 3′ = 0, L 3 3′ = 1. 10 27

# Page 14^page=14
Example - Part 3 Example Let K be a coordinate system with orthonormal basis i1, i2, i3. Let K′ be a new coordinate system with basis vectors e ′ 1 = i1, e ′ 2 = 2i2, e ′ 3 = i1 + i3. Consider the vector B over K with components B = (1, 1, 0) T . Compute the covariant components B′ i of B in the coordinate system K′. 11 27

# Page 15^page=15
Example - Part 4 Example The transformation rule gives B′ i = Lj i′Bj. We have shown L 1 1′ = 1, L 2 1′ = 0, L 3 1′ = 0, L 1 2′ = 0, L 2 2′ = 2, L 3 2′ = 0, L 1 3′ = 1, L 2 3′ = 0, L 3 3′ = 1. Thus, because B = (1, 1, 0)T we get B′ 1 = L j 1′Bj = L 1 1′B1 + L 2 1′B2 + L3 1′B3 = 1 + 0 + 0 = 1, B′ 2 = L j 2′Bj = L 1 2′B1 + L 2 2′B2 + L3 2′B3 = 0 + 2 + 0 = 2, B′ 3 = L j 3′Bj = L 1 3′B1 + L 2 3′B2 + L3 3′B3 = 1 + 0 + 0 = 1. 12 27

# Page 16^page=16
Example - Part 5 Example We can also ˝nd the coordinates of B ′ using matrices. We have L =  1 0 0 0 2 0 1 0 1   B =  1 1 0   . The transformation rule gives B′ i = Lj i′Bj. Thus, B′ = L · B =   1 0 0 0 2 0 1 0 1     1 1 0   =  1 2 1   . 13 27

# Page 17^page=17
The relationship between co- variant and contravariant components

# Page 18^page=18
Covariant to contravariant components - Dot product Recall: Expansions Recall we have the following two expansions: A = A1e1 + A2e2 + A 3e3 = Akek A = A1e 1 + A2e 2 + A3e 3 = Ake k How can we express the covariant components in terms of the contravariant components? First, take the scalar product with ei and ei, respectively: A · ei = Ak(ei · ek), A · e i = Ak(e i · e k). 14 27

# Page 19^page=19
Covariant to contravariant components - New notation New notation We have two expressions: A · ei = Ak(ei · ek), A · e i = Ak(e i · e k). To simplify notation, we write ei · ek = gik = gki, e i · e k = gik = gki, ei · e k = g.k i = { 0 if i ̸= k 1 if i = k. (Dual bases) 15 27

# Page 20^page=20
Covariant to contravariant components - Formula Covariant to contravariant components Thus, we can rewrite the expressions A · ei = Ak(ei · ek) and A · e i = Ak(e i · e k). using this new notation: A · ei = Akgik, and A · e i = Akgik. Recall that Ai = A · ei and Ai = A · ei. Thus, we conclude Ai = gikAk, Ai = gikAk. 16 27

# Page 21^page=21
Summary: Covariant to contravariant components Summary: Covariant to contravariant components We can express the covariant components Ai of a vector A in terms of is contravariant components Ai (and vice versa) using the formulas Ai = gikAk, Ai = gikAk, where gik = gki = ei · ek, gik = gki = e i · e k. 17 27

# Page 22^page=22
Example 1 - gij Example 1 Express the scalar product of two vectors A · B in terms of their covariant and contravariant components. Using di˙erent combinations of the formulae A = Aiei = Aiei and B = Bkek = Bkek, we see that A · B = Aiei · Bkek︸ ︷︷ ︸ contravariant = Aie i · Bke k ︸ ︷︷ ︸ covariant = Aie i · Bkek︸ ︷︷ ︸ mix = Aiei · Bke k ︸ ︷︷ ︸ mix , Hence, A · B = Aiei · Bkek = ei · ekAiBk = gikAiBk, = Aie i · Bke k = e i · e kAiBk = gikAiBk. 18 27

# Page 23^page=23
Example 1 - gij - Part 2 Example 1 We have shown A · B = gikAiBk, = gikAiBk. Now, since gikBk = Bi and gikBk = Bi, we obtain A · B = gikAiBk = AiBi, = gikAiBk = AiBi. 19 27

# Page 24^page=24
Example 2 Example 2 Express the cosine of the angle between two vectors in terms of their covariant and contravariant components. Recall that cos(A, B) = A·B |A||B| . (Practical 1) We have just found A · B = AiBi = AiBi. Then, we have: |A| = √A · A = √ AiAi, |B| = √B · B = √ BiBi. We conclude cos(A, B) = AiBi √ AiAi√ BiBi = AiBi√ AiAi√ BiBi . 20 27

# Page 25^page=25
Example 3 Example 3 Express the vector product A × B of two vectors in terms of their covariant and contravariant components. (That is, for C = A × B = Ciei what are the coe˚cients Ci?) Using A = Ajej and B = Bkek, we obtain in vector notation A × B =   3∑ j=1 Ajej   × ( 3∑ k=1 Bkek ) = 3∑ j,k=1 AjBk(ej × ek) 21 27

# Page 26^page=26
Example 3 - Part 2 Example 3 Continuing A × B = 3∑ j,k=1 AjBk(ej × ek) = A1B2(e1 × e2) + A1B3(e1 × e3) + A 2B3(e2 × e3) − A3B1(e1 × e3) − A3B2(e2 × e3) − A2B1(e1 × e2) = (A1B2 − A2B1)(e1 × e2) + (A1B3 − A3B1)(e1 × e3) + (A2B3 − A3B2)(e2 × e3) = ∑ i<j (AjBk − AkBj)(ej × ek). 22 27

# Page 27^page=27
Example 3 - Part 3 Example 3 We have so far A × B = ∑ i<j (AjBk − AkBj)(ej × ek). By de˝nition, V = ei · (ej × ek) is such that e i = ej × ek V thus ej × ek = V e i, whenever (i, j, k) is a cyclic permutation of (1, 2, 3). As a consequence C = A × B = (A1B2 − A2B1)(e1 × e2) + (A1B3 − A3B1)(e1 × e3) + (A 2B3 − A3B2)(e2 × e3) = (A jBk − A kBj)V e i = Cie i. 23 27

# Page 28^page=28
Example 3 - Part 4 Example 3 Consequently C = A × B = (A1B2 − A2B1)(e1 × e2) + (A1B3 − A3B1)(e1 × e3) + (A2B3 − A3B2)(e2 × e3) = (A1B2 − A2B1)(V e 3) + (A1B3 − A3B1)(−V e2) + (A2B3 − A 3B2)(V e1) = (A2B3 − A3B2)V e1 + (A 3B1 − A1B3)V e2 + (A1B2 − A2B1)V e 3. 24 27

# Page 29^page=29
Example 3 - Part 5 Example 3 Finally, notice that C = A × B = (A2B3 − A 3B2)V e1 + (A3B1 − A1B3)V e2 + (A1B2 − A2B1)V e 3 = ∑ (i,j,k) (AjBk − AkBj)V e i, where the sum ranges over all cyclic permutations of (1, 2, 3). Comparing this formula with C = Ciei, we see that Ci = (AjBk − AkBj), where (i, j, k) is a cyclic permutation of (1, 2, 3). 25 27

# Page 30^page=30
Practical question Your turn! Express the scalar triple product (A × B) · C in terms of the contravariant components of the vectors A, B and C, with respect to dual bases. That is A = Aiei, B = Biei, C = Ciei. You may use the result from the previous example: D = A × B = Die i = ∑ i (AjBk − AkBj)V e i where V = ei · (ej × ek) 26 27
